If I were to take a guess, the problem isn’t “AI wrote bad code.” Lots of us in tech have seen this pattern too many times. It’s more likely a failure in a process that they recently adopted and are failing to get maturity around. Let me explain, modern Agile pipelines are very good at checking whether individual tickets meet narrowly defined acceptance criteria, but much worse at asking whether the overall system still behaves coherently after hundreds of interconnected tickets have been completed. Requirements get fragmented across Jira tickets, Designers or BAs struggle to write them properly, devs are assigned who probably don’t even play computer games, QA validates against the ticket instead of the larger gameplay experience, sprint deadlines force partial solutions through, and you are left with something that wouldn’t even pass a beta test. Everyone can technically “do their job correctly” and still ship a hot mess because the process optimizes for throughput, not system stability. AI unironically actually helps this type development paradigm that Microsoft pushes hard on, but it’s still not enough, is it.

posts.name: Username
posts.cooked:
Thaile:

modern Agile pipelines are very good at checking whether

I agree with your broader Agile critique, but IMO agile itself is not inherently bad. Bad Agile is bad. When Agile becomes Jira throughput theater - close tickets, hit sprint commitments, ship increments, measure velocity - it can absolutely optimize for movement over coherence. In a game like Warcraft, that is especially dangerous because the product is not just a set of features. It is a connected experience.

That’s actually where the Windows 11 / Warcraft comparison I made earlier in the thread makes the most sense to me.

Both Warcraft and Windows are modern products sitting on top of extremely old, extremely complex foundations. Windows 11 still has decades of legacy Windows behavior underneath it. WoW still has twenty-plus years of engine assumptions, combat systems, UI layers, quest logic, itemization rules, phasing, instancing, addon hooks, and weird edge cases underneath it.

So when people say “why can’t they just fix it?” the answer is often: because there may not be a clean “just fix it.” A small change can interact with ancient assumptions nobody wants to touch because everything else depends on them. And because there is nobody there that completely understands them the way their creators did.

But that also strengthens the argument for slowing down. If you are working on a giant legacy system, you need more integration testing, more regression testing, more holistic QA, and more time between major changes - not less.

I see this dynamic playing out more often than I’d like. I use AI daily - part of my job in research and development (academia) is to find ways for clients to use the things properly.

In my experience, when AI fails inside one of our client company’s workflow, the failure almost never “the AI tool is bad.” A lot of the time, the AI is exposing that the organization does not actually understand its own process well enough to automate or augment it.

If your requirements are vague, your acceptance criteria are shallow, your QA is ticket-bound, your documentation is stale, your domain knowledge lives in people’s heads, and nobody has a coherent model of the whole system, then AI will not magically fix that. It will amplify the mess.

AI is very good at accelerating whatever the heck it is you give it to start with. It is much worse at rescuing an undefined one. Nine times out of 10 you’ll just make a huge mess that will take twice as long to untangle because not only did you never understand the problem you were trying to fix but also don’t understand the changes the ai recommended you make.

And that’s when they call me. But of course its not my job to explain to the client why they have a mess on their hands. I’m “an Oracle whisperer” not a “client whisperer” LOL

If I could, I would explain to them that when companies inject AI into their plumbing and it produces bad results, that is diagnostic. It reveals where the company was already relying on manual correction, vague judgment calls, and users catching what the process missed.

Sadly by the time I get there the CEO already laid off the only people there who really understand how they kept things running with a wad of chewing gum and some bailing wire.

I get to do a site visit on one of those next week and am dreading it.

Thaile:

The model does not literally become a senior engineer, but the prompt establishes behavioral framing more than the expertise itself, which is still there in the training data.

Cool. I think you get it! But there are layers of nuance - as there is with all good RP.

My compressed RP with ai doctrine:

  • Define the room.
  • Play your role.
  • Give the model a bounded cognitive task.
  • Move the problem through separate phases.
  • Harvest only canon.
  • Exit the frame before acting.

Most people think RP works because it constrains the AI.
My experience: RP works because it constrains the operator.

That is the thesis.

Role-play is not mainly a way to make AI “act like” something. It is a way to make YOU, the user, operate inside a coherent frame.

Most users put the model in costume: “You are my financial analyst,” “you are my expert project manager,” “you are Socratic,” “you are adversarial.” But they do not put themselves in role. Then they violate the frame. They ask for Socratic teaching but seek reassurance. They ask for adversarial review but punish disagreement. They ask for medical reasoning but demand treatment certainty. The AI detects the contradiction and the room collapses.

The power of RP is that it gives the operator discipline. The user defines the room, accepts the rules of that room, and behaves consistently enough that the model can infer the correct kind of intelligence to perform. This is not prompting. It is interaction choreography.

A good AI role-play frame does five things.

First, it defines jurisdiction: what this room is for, what it is not for, who has authority, what counts as evidence, and what must not happen here.

Second, it separates phases. Generation, interpretation, validation, and action should not happen in the same breath. When they collapse into one prompt, the result is confident sludge: the model brainstorms, validates itself, explains itself, and recommends action all at once. Better practice moves the problem through rooms. And each room has a defined hand-off.

Third, it preserves “RP” canon deliberately. Most AI output should not survive. Some is useful, some is seductive, some is wrong, and some is merely pretty. The operator’s job is to harvest only what earned its place, restart cleanly, and carry forward the durable artifact. Copy/paste. Rerun, copy/paste again. Rerun.

Fourth, it reduces ambiguity rather than manipulating the model. Bad RP tries to trick the system or bypass boundaries. Good RP makes intent legible: here is the classroom, here is the exercise, here is the boundary, here is the outside authority, and here is what we are not doing.

Fifth, it keeps authorship with the user. The strongest frame often makes the AI the student, not the expert. The operator remains the teacher, examiner, director, and editor. The model helps understand, test, articulate, and refine inside the user’s rubric.

The paradox is that boundaries create freedom. Vague freedom makes the model generic. Precise boundaries let it specialize. But the right constraints do not over-script the model’s imagination. They constrain failure modes.

This is how I learned to do RP in this game. And its the only reason I think I can get things out of ai (even non-LLM) effectively in situations where others struggle.

“Play an engineer on TV” is useful, but try this…

“we are staging an engineering review, and you (the model) are performing the engineer role inside a bounded room whose rules I must also obey.”

That shifts the lesson from persona imitation to frame governance.

Do this and the model is not the only actor in the scene. The model is also in role. It will have to behave like someone who genuinely wants senior-engineer review: clear requirements, acceptance of pushback, respect for edge cases, willingness to define tradeoffs, and no penalty for disagreement.

So the prompt is not “summon engineer.”

It is: “create an engineering review room and impress me by behaving consistently inside it.”

Then give it screen captures of everything you see as you work together through the exercise

Consider each screen cap as both state continuity but also a potential test of its careful competence and its approach to problem resolution.
